title: OCR retrieval: preserve reading order, page regions and uncertainty
summary: Index scanned documents as positioned evidence rather than flattening columns, captions and doubtful characters into one text stream.
body:
Index scanned documents as positioned evidence rather than flattening columns, captions and doubtful characters into one text stream.

Keep the page geometry

OCR retrieval searches text extracted from scans while preserving where each token appeared. The page image is the source; recognized text is a fallible interpretation. Store document revision, page number, bounding box, block type, reading-order position and extraction confidence with each passage. A two-column safety sheet can interleave warnings with unrelated specifications if its text is flattened by coordinate order alone. Extraction provenance should let a reviewer reopen the precise image region behind a candidate.

Reconstruct blocks before chunks

Detect headings, paragraphs, footnotes, tables and captions as separate blocks, then connect them in a plausible reading order. A caption can belong to a diagram beside it rather than the paragraph directly above it. Chunk within a block or a justified parent section; crossing column boundaries can invent a sentence that was never printed. Keep alternative reading-order hypotheses when a page is ambiguous. Hierarchical retrieval can route by section while leaving the cited evidence on the original page region.

Handle uncertain characters

A scan may confuse P-47 with P-41 or 83 kPa with 88 kPa. Record character- or token-level confidence when the OCR engine provides it. Exact-match retrieval of identifiers should search the recognized string and, within a bounded error budget, reviewed alternatives. Do not silently replace low-confidence digits with a fluent guess. For a numeric answer, require the number and unit to be legible in the image or verified by an independent source. Numeric cell context matters even when the table was recognized correctly.

Separate search from support

OCR text is useful for candidate generation, but an answer citing a scan needs a page and a region. A high ranking score cannot validate an illegible number. If a candidate's decisive token is below the review threshold, send the region to a human or abstain. Preserve redaction masks in both OCR text and image crops; otherwise a search result might expose text that the displayed image hides. Permission rules apply to page metadata and crops as well as text.

Judge image-grounded retrieval

Build queries for split columns, rotated labels, handwriting, captions, tables, near-identical part numbers and pages with no answer. Score page recall, region overlap, reading-order integrity and final claim support separately. A system that finds the correct PDF but cites the wrong column should fail. Record OCR engine and layout model versions so a model upgrade can be compared on exactly the same scanned pages. Review regressions on low-resolution and multilingual slices rather than accepting one aggregate score.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PageBlock:
    document_id: str
    page: int
    column: int
    order: int
    confidence: float
    text: str

def ordered_evidence(blocks: list[PageBlock], document_id: str,
                     minimum_confidence: float) -> list[PageBlock]:
    if not 0 <= minimum_confidence <= 1:
        raise ValueError("confidence threshold outside [0, 1]")
    eligible = [block for block in blocks if block.document_id == document_id
                and block.confidence >= minimum_confidence]
    return sorted(eligible, key=lambda block: (block.page, block.column, block.order))

scan = [PageBlock("manual-r4", 3, 2, 1, .97, "Pump P-47 limit: 83 kPa"),
        PageBlock("manual-r4", 3, 1, 1, .99, "Hydraulic system"),
        PageBlock("manual-r4", 3, 2, 2, .44, "Unclear value: 88?"),
        PageBlock("manual-r3", 3, 2, 1, .99, "Pump P-47 limit: 71 kPa")]
assert [block.text for block in ordered_evidence(scan, "manual-r4", .85)] == [
    "Hydraulic system", "Pump P-47 limit: 83 kPa"]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting B blocks costs O(B log B) time and O(B) output space. OCR and layout inference cost far more than the ordering operation, so cache extraction by document hash and model version. Crops, coordinates and alternate transcripts add storage. Higher-resolution rescans can improve evidence quality but increase processing and review cost; target them at low-confidence answer-bearing regions.

Common Mistakes

  • Concatenating two columns into a fabricated sentence.
  • Treating an OCR guess for a digit as verified evidence.
  • Citing only a PDF title when the answer lives in one page region.
  • Redacting the image but leaving its recognized text searchable.

Validation drill

Scan 47 pages with columns, tables and captions. Judge 37 questions and require page-region overlap, correct number and unit, and an abstention when the decisive characters remain uncertain.

title: Geospatial retrieval: combine meaning, distance and jurisdiction
summary: Find nearby eligible evidence with explicit coordinate systems, radius limits and geographic provenance.
body:
Find nearby eligible evidence with explicit coordinate systems, radius limits and geographic provenance.

Define what the location means

Geospatial retrieval finds records whose physical coverage matters to the query. 'Show repair notices near station P-47' could mean notices located at a point, assets within a radius, or policies applying to a jurisdiction polygon. Those are different predicates. Store geometry type, coordinate reference system, accuracy, valid interval and source identity with the record. A document mentioning a city name is not necessarily located there. Query routing should distinguish place intent from a text-only mention before choosing a spatial operation.

Filter space before semantic rank

Apply tenant permission, active revision and geographic eligibility before semantic ranking. A nearby restricted maintenance ticket should not appear in a result count, map marker or generated answer. Use an indexed radius predicate for point proximity, then compute exact distance for candidates; use containment or intersection for coverage areas. Do not compare raw latitude-longitude degree differences with a radius in meters. Corpus permissions remain part of the spatial query, not a presentation-layer patch.

Keep uncertainty visible

A geocoded address may identify a street rather than a building. A device location can drift; a service district boundary can change. Store location accuracy and boundary version, and avoid a definitive inside/outside claim when an uncertainty circle crosses the edge. For a 'within 2 km' question, state whether distance is straight-line, walking route or drive time. The retrieval result should include the location source and the calculated distance, so the claim can be checked. Temporal retrieval governs historical boundaries.

Combine place and text without score confusion

A spatial index can return a bounded set of eligible records, after which lexical or vector ranking identifies the relevant notice. For broad areas, text search may produce candidates first, followed by exact geometry checks. Choose order from selectivity and cost, but keep both filters mandatory. Ranking a notice highly cannot make an out-of-area record eligible. Do not merge kilometers and semantic similarity into one unexplained scalar. Source budgets can reserve results across nearby notices and region-wide rules.

Test boundaries, not just centers

Judge cases on both sides of a district border, exactly at the radius, with missing coordinates, stale geocodes, overlapping regions and different tenant scopes. Report eligible-record recall separately from relevance and answer support. Include a named location that appears in a document body but lies outside its service area. A system that finds the right topic and wrong jurisdiction must fail even if its prose sounds plausible. Capture geometry version and distance method in the evaluation trace.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import asin, cos, radians, sin, sqrt

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ServiceNotice:
    notice_id: str
    tenant: str
    latitude: float
    longitude: float
    text: str

def distance_km(lat_a: float, lon_a: float, lat_b: float, lon_b: float) -> float:
    if any(not -90 <= lat <= 90 for lat in (lat_a, lat_b)):
        raise ValueError("invalid latitude")
    if any(not -180 <= lon <= 180 for lon in (lon_a, lon_b)):
        raise ValueError("invalid longitude")
    north = radians(lat_b - lat_a)
    east = radians(lon_b - lon_a)
    arc = sin(north / 2) ** 2 + cos(radians(lat_a)) * cos(radians(lat_b)) * sin(east / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * 6371.0088 * asin(min(1.0, sqrt(arc)))

def nearby(notices: list[ServiceNotice], tenant: str,
           latitude: float, longitude: float, radius_km: float) -> list[str]:
    if radius_km < 0:
        raise ValueError("negative radius")
    return [notice.notice_id for notice in notices if notice.tenant == tenant
            and distance_km(latitude, longitude, notice.latitude, notice.longitude) <= radius_km]

notices = [ServiceNotice("pump-47", "north", 28.6139, 77.2090, "Valve inspection"),
           ServiceNotice("pump-83", "north", 28.7041, 77.1025, "Valve inspection"),
           ServiceNotice("private", "south", 28.6139, 77.2090, "Valve inspection")]
assert nearby(notices, "north", 28.6139, 77.2090, 2) == ["pump-47"]

Performance and operating cost

The transparent scan costs O(N) distance calculations and O(K) output space for K matches. A spatial index narrows large corpora before exact distance checks; maintaining it adds storage and write work. Haversine computes a spherical straight-line approximation, not route distance or polygon coverage. Use a geography-aware database predicate for production radius searches and measure boundary errors where accuracy matters.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing coordinate degrees directly with kilometers.
  • Treating a place name in text as a verified record location.
  • Filtering geography after showing restricted candidate metadata.
  • Ignoring location uncertainty near a boundary.

Validation drill

Prepare 61 notices across two districts with five missing geocodes and seven boundary cases. Compare point-radius and jurisdiction queries, reporting eligible recall, false inclusions and supported location claims.

title: Database retrieval: link a question to schema and trace the rows
summary: Retrieve structured answers with approved query plans, row-level permissions and verifiable source identifiers.
body:
Retrieve structured answers with approved query plans, row-level permissions and verifiable source identifiers.

Retrieve a schema contract first

Database retrieval maps a question to tables, columns, joins and filters before reading rows. A request for unpaid invoices from branch 47 should identify invoice status, branch ID and billing date; an embedding over column descriptions may help discover candidates but cannot define the final join. Store approved schema descriptions, key relationships and field meanings. A column named amount may be gross, net or settled. Intent routing should distinguish a row lookup from a policy explanation or a calculation.

Keep query generation bounded

Treat a proposed SQL query as untrusted input. Constrain it to an allowlisted read-only view or a small set of approved query templates. Bind values as parameters, cap rows and time, and reject mutations or cross-tenant joins. Parsing a generated string for the word SELECT alone is not a security boundary; database permissions and row-level security must enforce scope. Access control belongs at the data source as well as in the retrieval layer.

Carry row provenance into the answer

Return primary keys, source table or view, query template version, data snapshot and effective filters with each result. An aggregate such as '47 unpaid invoices' needs a traceable query and the population definition, not merely a plausible sentence. If a join multiplies rows, count distinct invoice IDs or fix the join before answering. For a cell-level claim, identify both the row and column. Table evidence requires the unit and row context that make a number meaningful.

Separate retrieval from computation

A row set may require arithmetic after retrieval, but that computation should be deterministic and reviewable. Currency conversion needs an explicit rate and as-of date; a missing rate should cause a partial answer or abstention. A result that combines transactional rows with a document policy needs separate citations to each source. Evidence chains should show which source supplies the rule and which supplies the transaction facts.

Evaluate query and result failures

Judge schema linking, authorized row recall, predicate accuracy, join cardinality and final answer support separately. Include duplicate line items, soft-deleted records, null status, renamed columns and time-zone boundaries. A syntactically valid query can be semantically wrong: selecting posted_at instead of due_at may produce credible but incorrect overdue counts. Compare the executed query and returned row IDs against a reviewed reference set; do not grade only the final prose.

Worked contract

import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE invoices (invoice_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, tenant TEXT, branch INTEGER, status TEXT, amount_cents INTEGER)")
connection.executemany("INSERT INTO invoices VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    ("INV-47", "north", 47, "unpaid", 8300),
    ("INV-48", "north", 47, "paid", 4700),
    ("INV-49", "south", 47, "unpaid", 9900),
])

def unpaid_invoices(tenant: str, branch: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    return connection.execute(
        "SELECT invoice_id, amount_cents FROM invoices "
        "WHERE tenant = ? AND branch = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY invoice_id LIMIT 83",
        (tenant, branch, "unpaid"),
    ).fetchall()

assert unpaid_invoices("north", 47) == [("INV-47", 8300)]
connection.close()

Performance and operating cost

With an index on tenant, branch and status, a selective lookup can avoid scanning every invoice; the exact cost depends on the planner and row count. The in-memory example is tiny, but a production read needs a row cap, execution timeout and query plan check. Materializing R result rows costs O(R) memory; stream large exports rather than placing them in an answer context.

Common Mistakes

  • Executing free-form generated SQL with broad database privileges.
  • Using a similarly named amount column without checking its business definition.
  • Counting joined line items as distinct invoices.
  • Omitting row IDs and filter values from an aggregate's audit trace.

Validation drill

Create 43 questions against invoices, payments and branch tables. Include duplicate line items, nulls and two tenants. Require matching row IDs, approved schema paths, correct aggregate populations and no cross-tenant disclosure.

title: Conversational retrieval: rewrite the follow-up without changing its scope
summary: Resolve references in a dialogue while carrying only the constraints that still apply to the current search turn.
body:
Resolve references in a dialogue while carrying only the constraints that still apply to the current search turn.

Make the current turn searchable

Conversational retrieval turns a context-dependent follow-up into a standalone search request. After 'What is the P-47 limit in revision r4?', 'What about the old one?' may refer to the same pump and a prior revision. A rewrite should capture that relation without inventing a date or unit. Keep the raw user text, the selected antecedent and the resolved query in the trace. Query routing should use the resolved intent only after checking that the reference is unambiguous.

Carry constraints with expiration

Tenant identity and authorization come from the active session, never from an earlier answer string. Topic, entity and date constraints may carry forward for one turn, but they can also be overridden. 'Now compare P-48' replaces P-47; 'in the south plant' changes place but must not grant access to south-plant records. Track each constraint's origin, confidence and scope, then apply explicit user changes before searching. Conversation caches need the resulting permission and constraint identity in their keys.

Ask when reference resolution is unsafe

'What about that one?' may point to two passages from the previous answer. Picking one silently can produce a well-cited answer to the wrong question. Clarify when multiple antecedents remain plausible, or search both only if a comparison was requested and permissions allow both. Do not use the last retrieved passage as the default referent merely because it was ranked first. A bounded clarification step is cheaper than a confident but irrelevant retrieval. Abstention also applies to unresolved dialogue state.

Prevent answer contamination

The previous assistant answer may be wrong, incomplete or injected. Rewrites should rely on authenticated conversation metadata and user turns, then retrieve fresh source evidence. Do not copy a previous answer's unsupported number into the next query as though it were a fact. When the user asks 'why did that change?', retrieve both applicable revisions and compare their cited text. Temporal retrieval preserves the two evidence sets rather than blending old and new values.

Judge turn-by-turn retrieval

Evaluate follow-ups with pronouns, topic switches, corrections, permission changes, long gaps and contradictory prior answers. Score resolved entity and constraints before measuring passage recall and final support. A system can retrieve the correct passage for a wrong rewrite by luck; that should not hide the rewrite defect. Store the conversation turn ID and corpus generation in the trace. When a user revokes or changes scope, previously cached passages must not reappear in later turns.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchTurn:
    entity: str | None
    revision: str | None
    tenant: str

def resolve_follow_up(previous: SearchTurn, current_text: str,
                      active_tenant: str) -> SearchTurn:
    text = current_text.casefold()
    if "p-48" in text:
        entity = "P-48"
    elif "p-47" in text:
        entity = "P-47"
    elif "old one" in text and previous.entity:
        entity = previous.entity
    else:
        raise ValueError("ambiguous entity; ask for clarification")
    revision = "previous" if "old one" in text else None
    return SearchTurn(entity, revision, active_tenant)

last_turn = SearchTurn("P-47", "r4", "north")
assert resolve_follow_up(last_turn, "What about the old one?", "north") == SearchTurn(
    "P-47", "previous", "north")
assert resolve_follow_up(last_turn, "Now compare P-48", "north") == SearchTurn(
    "P-48", None, "north")

Performance and operating cost

The example resolves one turn in O(L) time for text length L and O(1) additional state. A production resolver may inspect a bounded window of T turns, increasing work with that window and with each retrieval retry. Avoid feeding the entire dialogue into every search when only an explicit entity and recent correction are needed. Record and evaluate clarification frequency as part of latency and success.

Common Mistakes

  • Carrying an old entity after the user explicitly switched topics.
  • Treating a prior assistant answer as a verified source for the next query.
  • Taking tenant access from dialogue text instead of the active session.
  • Resolving an ambiguous pronoun to the first-ranked passage without asking.

Validation drill

Write 59 multi-turn queries with corrections, topic changes and ambiguous references. Record rewrite accuracy, authorized passage recall and final support, and require clarification for turns with no unique antecedent.

  • Temporal retrieval: answer as-of questions from valid evidence
  • Grounded answers: require passage support and a no-answer path

title: Document extraction: preserve passage provenance through OCR and parsing
summary: Turn source files into searchable passages while retaining the page, section, revision and extraction quality needed to verify an answer.
body:
Turn source files into searchable passages while retaining the page, section, revision and extraction quality needed to verify an answer.

Define the extracted record

A text string alone is not a source. Each passage needs document ID, immutable revision ID, page or section, span offsets when available, extraction method, language and access label. A PDF policy may contain a scanned page, two-column layout and a table whose cells change meaning when read in the wrong order. Store the source file hash and parser version so a changed extraction can be rebuilt without pretending the document itself changed. Corpus identity is the parent contract.

Separate clean text from uncertain text

Parse machine-readable text first. Route image-only pages to OCR, and mark uncertain spans rather than silently normalizing them into authoritative policy. A table value of 47 under ‘hours’ is different from 47 under ‘days’; flattening the headers can invert a support rule. Keep table headers with row text or represent the table as structured cells. Human review should focus on low-confidence pages that answer high-impact questions, not every document equally.

Retain location through cleanup

Whitespace normalization, header removal and dehyphenation can improve search. They also shift character offsets. Maintain a map from cleaned spans back to source-page coordinates or stable section IDs. When the answer cites a passage, the reader should land on the source location that actually supports the claim. If an OCR run changes, rebuild the chunk IDs and invalidate answers tied to old offsets. Citation integrity depends on this map.

Gate ingestion with concrete failures

Feed the parser a missing page, duplicate footer, rotated scan, repeated table header and an inaccessible file. Reject a document if its required metadata or access label is absent. Record page count, extracted character count, empty pages and confidence distribution. A parser yielding text is not evidence that it preserved meaning. Compare a reviewed sample of passages against the original page, especially around headings, tables and footnotes.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExtractedPassage:
    document_id: str
    revision_id: str
    page: int
    section: str
    text: str
    source_sha256: str

def passage_record(document_id: str, revision_id: str, page: int,
                   section: str, text: str, source_bytes: bytes) -> ExtractedPassage:
    if page < 1 or not document_id or not revision_id or not section or not text.strip():
        raise ValueError("incomplete extraction provenance")
    return ExtractedPassage(document_id, revision_id, page, section,
                            text.strip(), sha256(source_bytes).hexdigest())

source = b"Policy r8 page 4"
passage = passage_record("refund-policy", "r8", 4, "Exceptions", " 47 hours ", source)
assert passage.page == 4 and passage.text == "47 hours"
assert passage.source_sha256 == sha256(source).hexdigest()

Performance and operating cost

Extraction is O(B) in source bytes before OCR; OCR cost also depends on page count and resolution. Provenance adds small metadata per passage, while page images and offset maps add storage. Budget retries by document, not an unbounded queue. Measure empty-page rate and reviewed semantic errors separately from parser throughput.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating OCR output as exact text without a confidence or review path.
  • Dropping table headers or section titles before chunking.
  • Reusing offsets after normalization changes the text.
  • Indexing a passage when its access label or revision is missing.

Validation drill

Extract a 23-page policy with a two-column page, one rotated scan and a table. Check five answer-bearing passages against their original page and record which parser change would invalidate each citation.

title: Retrieval query routing: preserve exact constraints before search
summary: Route identifiers, policy questions and aggregate requests to the right evidence path without rewriting away the user's constraints.
body:
Route identifiers, policy questions and aggregate requests to the right evidence path without rewriting away the user's constraints.

Classify the request before reformulation

A question containing case ID AX-47 and an exact error string needs a literal lookup; a paraphrase of a policy may need semantic retrieval. A count of cases by week belongs to a governed query over structured data. Treat these as different jobs. Extract the requested output, exact tokens, tenant scope and time boundary first. A reformulator may add synonyms, but it cannot replace AX-47 with a more common case or turn a count into a prose summary. Candidate retrieval starts after this contract is fixed.

Keep routing observable

Record the selected path and the reason: exact ID, natural-language passage, structured aggregation, or mixed evidence. Run lexical and semantic search in parallel for mixed requests, then merge permitted candidates. A vector match can help find related language, but it cannot establish that a literal identifier was present. If a required identifier is absent from the result, reject that candidate even when its embedding score is high. A SQL query must use an approved metric definition; generated SQL is not a substitute for permission checks.

Handle ambiguous follow-ups

For ‘What changed after that?’, resolve ‘that’ from the current conversation only when a single permitted document identity is clear. Carry the resolved ID, revision and time window into the new query. If two incidents were discussed, ask which one the user means. Never copy a previous user's context or a past authorization decision into a new session. Conversation boundaries need the same rigor as document permissions.

Evaluate the router as a component

Create a labeled set with identifiers, paraphrases, mixed questions, unsupported aggregates and ambiguous follow-ups. Count wrong-route decisions separately from search misses. An exact-search route can fail because the identifier was parsed incorrectly; a semantic route can fail because its candidate pool omitted the answer. Store the original query beside the routed form so reviewers can see what changed. Include at least one question where no source is eligible and require the no-answer path.

Worked contract

def route_support_query(question: str, case_ids: set[str]) -> dict[str, object]:
    import re
    requested_ids = set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", question.upper()))
    unknown_ids = requested_ids - case_ids
    if unknown_ids:
        return {"route": "no_match", "ids": sorted(unknown_ids)}
    if re.search(r"\b(count|how many|per week)\b", question.lower()):
        return {"route": "aggregate", "ids": sorted(requested_ids)}
    if requested_ids:
        return {"route": "hybrid_exact_first", "ids": sorted(requested_ids)}
    return {"route": "semantic", "ids": []}

known_cases = {"AX-47", "AX-63"}
assert route_support_query("Why did AX-47 retry?", known_cases)["route"] == "hybrid_exact_first"
assert route_support_query("Count AX-63 cases per week", known_cases)["route"] == "aggregate"
assert route_support_query("Explain AX-91", known_cases)["route"] == "no_match"

Performance and operating cost

Routing costs O(q + m) time for query length q and m extracted IDs in this small example. The expensive work is downstream: two search legs, an aggregation or a clarification turn. Log wrong-route rates by query family and cap simultaneous searches; a cheap router that silently drops an exact constraint wastes the entire answer pipeline.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating an embedding score as proof of an exact case-ID match.
  • Rewriting a user-specified date or identifier without retaining the original constraint.
  • Sending an aggregate question to passage search and inventing a count from snippets.
  • Resolving an ambiguous follow-up from a different session.

Validation drill

Build 47 labeled queries: 12 exact IDs, 12 paraphrases, 11 mixed requests, six aggregates and six ambiguous follow-ups. Report route accuracy for each family and inspect every false route before changing a threshold.

title: Table retrieval: keep numeric cells attached to their labels
summary: Retrieve tabular evidence without losing row keys, column units, revision dates or the calculation needed for an answer.
body:
Retrieve tabular evidence without losing row keys, column units, revision dates or the calculation needed for an answer.

Treat a cell as a qualified fact

The value 47 has no useful meaning alone. A searchable fact needs table ID, revision, row key, column name, unit, effective period and access label. Store a compact row rendering for discovery, but preserve typed cells for comparison and arithmetic. A question about the West queue's 47-hour target must not match a North queue row or a 47-day retention policy. Extraction provenance should point back to the original table location.

Separate discovery from computation

Use lexical or semantic search to locate a candidate table, then execute an approved operation over its typed rows. Do not derive a total by reading the top few text snippets; omitted rows silently bias the result. Exact row and column filters should run before aggregation. If the requested metric is not defined, ask for the metric rather than inventing a sum. Record the row IDs used so the answer can be audited after a table revision.

Handle headers and units

Merged headings, repeated page headers and blank cells need explicit parsing rules. A blank value can mean unknown, not zero. A percentage column cannot be summed like a count, and a currency column cannot be combined across currencies without a declared conversion rule. If a table changes from hours to minutes in a new revision, the retrieval layer must not silently mix both. Index swaps should move the searchable row text and typed table together.

Test answer coverage

Judged queries should include an exact cell lookup, a filter plus sum, a percentage with denominator, a missing cell and a superseded revision. Evaluate table discovery separately from calculation correctness. A system that retrieves the right table but adds the wrong rows still fails. For each calculated answer, retain the operation, selected row keys, table revision and resulting value.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class QueueRow:
    region: str
    week: int
    resolved: int | None
    revision: str

def resolved_total(rows: list[QueueRow], region: str, weeks: set[int],
                   revision: str) -> int:
    selected = [row for row in rows if row.region == region
                and row.week in weeks and row.revision == revision]
    if len(selected) != len(weeks) or any(row.resolved is None for row in selected):
        raise ValueError("incomplete table coverage")
    if len({row.week for row in selected}) != len(selected):
        raise ValueError("duplicate row key")
    return sum(row.resolved for row in selected if row.resolved is not None)

queue_rows = [QueueRow("West", 31, 47, "r8"),
              QueueRow("West", 32, 29, "r8"),
              QueueRow("North", 31, 81, "r8")]
assert resolved_total(queue_rows, "West", {31, 32}, "r8") == 76
try:
    resolved_total(queue_rows, "West", {31, 33}, "r8")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("missing week was accepted")

Performance and operating cost

The baseline scans N rows in O(N) time and stores O(K) selected rows. A typed index on revision, region and week avoids a full scan in a large warehouse; query cost then depends on matching rows and index lookup. Preserve row lineage even if it adds metadata, because a wrong numeric answer is harder to diagnose than a slow lookup.

Common Mistakes

  • Embedding isolated numeric cells without their row and column labels.
  • Treating blank cells as zero during aggregation.
  • Summing a top-k snippet sample instead of the full filtered table.
  • Combining rows from different revisions or units.

Validation drill

Build a 29-row queue table with two revisions and three regions. Answer 12 cell questions and eight aggregate questions. Make two cells blank and one row duplicated; require explicit errors for both cases.
